query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing in-situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder will result in reduced compositional segregation, lower residual thermal stresses, and fewer processing defects, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity compared to conventionally fabricated parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powder produced as pre-alloyed feedstock.
generation.intervention: Apply in-situ substrate preheating during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied under rapid solidification conditions typical of laser-based powder bed fusion, with layer thickness and scan rates comparable to conventional builds but with an elevated substrate temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients and moderated cooling rates resulting in more homogeneous microstructure and diminished segregation.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate increases the base temperature during deposition, which lowers the cooling rate and minimizes thermal gradients. This reduction diminishes compositional segregation, alleviates residual stresses, and reduces defect formation arising from rapid solidification.
generation.predicted_outcome: A directional improvement in mechanical integrity is anticipated, characterized by a more homogeneous microstructure, reduced residual stresses, and fewer defects when compared to parts fabricated conventionally (with a cold substrate). The exact magnitude of these improvements is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Conventional additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi using a standard (cold) substrate, which typically exhibits noticeable compositional segregation, high residual stresses, and enhanced defect density.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold for AM processes operating within similar energy density, layer thickness, and scan speed conditions, where residual thermal gradients are significant. The hypothesis may not extend to low cooling rate processes such as slow furnace cooling or isothermal sintering.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement levels (exact percentage reductions in segregation, stress, and defect density) are not precisely known, though consistent directional improvements are predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled AM fabrication study where identical AlCrFeNiSi specimens are built under two conditions: with in-situ substrate preheating and with a conventional cold substrate. Evaluate the cooling rates in-situ and, post-fabrication, analyze microstructural homogeneity, residual stresses, and defect density using standardized techniques.
measurements: Residual stress measurements (using X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction)
Microstructural and compositional analysis (using SEM/EDS and EBSD)
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and fracture toughness tests)
Thermal gradient monitoring during the build process
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens manufactured with substrate preheating do not show statistically significant reductions in compositional segregation, residual stresses, and processing defects—or if their mechanical properties are not improved relative to the conventionally fabricated specimens—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While substantial research has explored the L-PBF of high-entropy alloys, this work on CoCrFeNiCu addresses a critical gap by focusing on hot-cracking susceptibility at relatively low laser powers, a parameter space that has received limited attention in prior studies, which often prioritize density or mechanical properties without deeply investigating crack formation mechanisms. In contrast, our study on CoCrFeNiCu HEAs processed by L-PBF also observed hot cracking that could not be mitigated by process parameter adjustment, but the addition of Cu may influence the solidification behavior and residual stress distribution differently than in the equimolar CoCrFeNi system []. Furthermore, while previous work has shown that cracks are often located at high-angle grain boundaries and are linked to regions of high mechanical solicitation during solidification [], our in situ mechanical testing provides new insights into how these cracks behave under load, which has not been extensively reported for Cu-containing HEAs.

cited_evidence.text: Microsections were prepared and throughout the initial investigation, samples with noteworthy lack of fusion defects or significant keyhole porosity were ruled out. In addition to these defects, large horizontal cracks were seen as critical defects, disrupting the fabrication process due to the deterioration of the thermal conductivity towards the substrate plate, as well as the possible detachment of entire sections. Therefore, the initial set of 16 samples was reduced to four samples, which exhibited large defect-free sections, and the defects present were predominantly limited to vertical cracking (Figure 6). Vertical cracks were expected due to the absence of preheating (substrate plate preheating was not employed), coupled with the larger than usual layer thickness. Raising the build space temperature to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients is the most common approach to minimize cracking. New research also suggests that high-frequency laser power modulation is a suitable approach to prevent cracking []. decision.trend: Over the past several years, research on HEAs via additive manufacturing has focused on tailoring processing routes rather than altering compositions. Early work with refractory HEAs (PMC6427779, PMC8201384) demonstrated that SLM/PBF-LB/M can yield single-phase microstructures with acceptable levels of segregation by careful management of laser energy inputs. Subsequent studies (PMC9736672, PMC12250662) showed that fine‐tuning process parameters such as laser power and scan speed can partially alleviate defects and reduce residual stresses. However, even with optimized energy density, rapid solidification inherent to these methods still leads to compositional nonuniformities, high thermal gradients, and defect formation. Thus, while incremental gains have been achieved by tweaking laser parameters, the simultaneous control of segregation, residual stress, and defect formation remains a challenge.
decision.unsolved: A single processing intervention that can concurrently lessen compositional segregation, reduce residual thermal stresses, and minimize defects in cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi during rapid solidification has not yet been demonstrated.
decision.lever: implement in-situ substrate preheating during additive manufacturing
decision.why: In-situ platform preheating is a logical next step because it directly addresses the root causes of the observed issues. By raising the substrate temperature, the cooling rate is moderated and thermal gradients are reduced, which can decrease both compositional segregation and residual stresses, while also limiting the formation of processing defects. This intervention follows naturally from the trend where adjusting laser parameters has yielded improvements, and it offers a single, focused processing modification applicable to the cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi feedstock within the rapid solidification regime.
